title: If You Want to Get Rich With AI, Build This One Agent First
key_points: The speaker identifies Manis as the most powerful AI agent they've used, having also tested Claude Code, Codex, and Claude Co
The speaker claims to have made close to seven figures using AI and runs a company called Future IQ
Agentic AI differs from chat-level AI: it thinks, plans, opens tabs, writes code, pulls data, and completes full projects autonomously
Algorithmic leverage is defined as the strategic replacement of human labor with custom code and automation systems that run 24/7 without a team
The architect vs operator distinction: operators ask AI to write an email; architects tell AI to handle entire client outreach for the week and have it ready for review
Manis example given: typing one sentence to research top three AI coaches in a niche, pull their pricing, main offers, and top complaints from comment sections, then build a one-page summary
After initial Manis task completion, the speaker extends it to add testimonies, send links to assistant in Slack, and email copies to team with notes
A woman in the speaker's community built a downloadable web tool for a healthcare physician office that changed how her hospital runs protocol
Another person built a full CRM over a few months by directing Manis piece by piece, without knowing how to code
AI agents use tokens which cost money, and the agent does not get it right the first time — it runs, hits errors, tries again, rebuilds
The speaker has watched people drop $200, $300, even $500 in a weekend trying to build one tool because they did not understand how token costs work
Cost-saving strategy 1: Never start on a paid agent with vague ideas — write specifics including outcome, who it's for, what finished thing looks like, must-haves, and nice-to-haves
Cost-saving strategy 2: Practice on free tiers and free chat versions first to learn how to give directions and understand how agents think before moving to paid agents
Cost-saving strategy 3: Break work into small pieces rather than asking agent to build whole CRM in one shot — build first screen, test it, then next
Security concern addressed: start with low-risk tasks first like research, drafts, internal documents before letting agent touch anything sensitive
AI slop in equals AI slop out: output quality matches direction quality — the tool does not fix you, it scales you
Manis has been acquired; the speaker acknowledges uncertainty about what that means long-term for the tool
The skills of direction, specification writing, and review transfer to whatever new tool emerges — the skill is the asset, the tool is just the tool
The playbook is stated as: outcome, instructions, review, repeat
summary:
Aduina McKennon, who has been featured in Forbes as an AI business strategist and runs Future IQ, claims to have made close to seven figures using AI. She states her mission is to help 50 million people learn to use AI to build wealth and businesses. She positions this video as revealing the truth about what AI agents actually cost to run, which she says most platforms hide while selling the dream.

The speaker introduces the concept of moving from chat-level AI use (asking questions and getting answers) to agentic AI, where the AI thinks, plans, opens tabs, writes code, pulls data, and completes entire projects autonomously. She introduces 'algorithmic leverage' as the strategic replacement of human labor with custom code and automation systems running 24/7 without a team. The key mindset shift is from being an 'operator' who asks AI to do individual tasks to being an 'architect' who sets direction, checks work, and approves results. She states this is the difference between a six-figure ceiling and an eight-figure run.

The specific tool recommended is Manis, which the speaker says does the full job rather than part of it. She gives a concrete example: typing one sentence asking Manis to research top three AI coaches in a niche, pull their pricing, main offers, and top complaints from comment sections, then build a one-page summary. She describes then extending this to have Manis add testimonies, send links to her assistant in Slack, and email copies to her team with notes. She cites community examples: a woman who built a downloadable web tool for a healthcare physician office, and another person who built a full CRM over months by directing Manis piece by piece — neither of whom knew how to code.

The video then addresses costs directly. The speaker explains that agents use tokens which cost money, and agents don't get it right the first time — they run, hit errors, try again, and rebuild. She states she has watched people drop $200, $300, even $500 in a weekend trying to build one tool. Her three cost-saving strategies are: never start on paid agents with vague ideas (write specifics including outcome, audience, finished product appearance, must-haves, nice-to-haves); practice on free tiers first to learn how to communicate with agents; break work into small pieces rather than building whole projects at once.

Addressing skeptics, she recommends starting with low-risk tasks for security concerns, acknowledges that weak goals produce weak outputs (the tool scales you, doesn't fix you), advises using agents as first drafts rather than sole sources for serious decisions, and confirms Manis has been acquired while noting the skills learned transfer to future tools. She concludes that winning with AI requires clear thinking, defined outcomes, clean instructions, and the ability to spot insufficient work — skills from managing teams, running projects, or raising children. The playbook is summarized as: outcome, instructions, review, repeat.
